title: Aranya Kāṇḍa: The Deep Forest and the Shadow of Evil
body:
Aranya Kāṇḍa: The Deep Forest and the Shadow of Evil

Virādha’s End

With Bharata gone home and the affairs of Ayodhyā settled as far as they could be settled, the three exiles left Chitrakūṭa. They had loved the green hill, but its peace had been broken by the coming and going of the great host, and more than that, Rāma felt that they should go deeper into the wild, away from the northern country and its constant reminders of all they had lost, into the true forest where the fourteen years could be lived as the fourteen years were meant to be lived. So they turned south, toward the vast Daṇḍaka forest, the deep and dangerous wilderness where the sages kept their scattered hermitages and the demons hunted them, and where the real trials of the exile awaited.

And almost at the threshold of that deeper forest, they met the first of its horrors.

His name was Virādha, and he was a demon of terrible size and strength, a monstrous shape that came crashing out of the trees upon them, huge, hideous, roaring, a giant of the wild places who fed on flesh and terrorized all who entered his domain. He fell upon the three of them without warning, and before they could well grasp what was happening, he had seized Sītā, snatched her up in his monstrous arms, and stood bellowing his defiance at the two brothers, threatening to devour them all.

For a moment even Rāma and Lakshmaṇa were at a loss, for the creature had Sītā, and any attack upon him risked her, and his size and fury were beyond anything they had yet faced. But the brothers were not the sort to be paralyzed for long, and they set upon the demon with their weapons, loosing arrow after arrow into his vast body, striking him with everything they had.

And here they met a horror worse than his size: he could not be killed. The arrows struck him and wounded him and did not slay him, for Virādha bore a boon that made him proof against death by weapons; no blade, no shaft, no missile could end his life. The brothers poured their whole strength into the assault, and the demon bled and roared and did not die, and for a terrible while it seemed that they had met an enemy that could not be overcome, one who would wear them down and devour them however hard they fought, because the ordinary means of his defeat were closed to them.

But Rāma and Lakshmaṇa were not only strong; they were resourceful, and where force alone would not serve, they found another way. If the demon could not be killed by weapons, then they would not try to kill him by weapons. They fell upon him instead with their bare hands and their whole bodies, and they overpowered him by main strength, and they cast him down, and finding that they could not slay him, they resolved to bury him, for a boon against weapons is no boon against the weight of the earth. They dug a great pit, and into it they cast the raging demon, and they buried him alive, heaping the earth upon him, so that the creature who could not be killed by any blade was ended after all, smothered in the ground, defeated by the one means his boon had not foreseen.

And then a wonder happened, for as the demon died beneath the earth, his monstrous form fell away, and out of it rose a being of light, a Gandharva, a celestial spirit, freed at last from a horrible shape. For Virādha had not always been a demon. He had once been a Gandharva of the heavens, and had been cursed, for some old offence, to wander the earth in that hideous monstrous form until Rāma should release him from it by death. His whole terrible existence as the demon Virādha had been a curse and a waiting, and the moment of his death at Rāma’s hands was the moment of his liberation, the breaking of the curse, the restoration of his true and radiant nature. He rose up freed and grateful, blessed the prince who had released him, and ascended to the celestial regions from which he had so long been exiled.

Let us pause on the pattern here, for it is one that runs all through this forest portion of the story, and it is worth understanding. Again and again, in the Daṇḍaka and beyond, Rāma will encounter a monster, and the monster will prove to be a cursed being in disguise, and Rāma’s slaying of it will turn out to be not a destruction but a redemption, the freeing of a trapped soul from a shape it was condemned to wear. Virādha is the first of these, and Kabandha will be another, and there are more. And the pattern carries a deep meaning. It tells us that what looks like Rāma’s violence is really Rāma’s grace; that the demons he destroys are, many of them, souls in torment waiting to be released; that the divine, even when it comes wielding weapons and dealing death, comes fundamentally to liberate, to free the bound, to restore the fallen to their true nature. Virādha the monster was Rāma’s enemy for an hour; Virādha the Gandharva was Rāma’s beneficiary forever; and the arrow, or in this case the burial, that ended the one was the very thing that freed the other. The forest is full of such transformations, and they teach us to look past the monstrous surface of things to the trapped soul that may lie beneath, and to understand that even the hardest and most violent-seeming acts of the divine are, at their root, acts of deliverance.

Now this whole episode, the tellers note, was one that Vishṇu Sreenivas had passed over in the condensed telling, moving the exiles from Chitrakūṭa toward Panchavaṭī without the encounter that in the fuller tradition marks their entry into the deep forest. But it belongs, and it is restored here, for it sets the note that the whole Araṇya Kāṇḍa will sound: that the peace of Chitrakūṭa is behind them now, that the forest ahead is a place of monsters and of magic, of terrible dangers and hidden redemptions, and that Rāma’s passage through it will be a long campaign against the powers of darkness that have made the wild a place of terror for the holy and the innocent. Virādha is the gate through which they pass out of the gentler exile and into the true wilderness, and his death and liberation are the first sounding of the theme that will build, chapter by chapter, toward the great confrontation with the lord of all the demons that waits at the far end of the forest road.

The three went on, then, past the buried demon and the freed spirit, deeper into the Daṇḍaka, toward the scattered hermitages of the sages who dwelt in that dangerous country, and toward the long quiet years, and the fateful meeting, that still lay ahead of them in the green and perilous heart of the wild.

Ten Years Pass

The years of the exile flowed by, and most of them flowed quietly, and the story, which lingers so long over single days of crisis, passes lightly over these long peaceful stretches, as memory itself passes lightly over the years in which nothing terrible happens. Ten of the fourteen years went by in the deep forest, and they were not, for the most part, years of horror, but years of a strange and simple grace.

For the exiles did not live all this while in one place. They moved through the Daṇḍaka from hermitage to hermitage, spending seasons here and seasons there, guests of the many sages who had made their homes in that wild country, and everywhere they went they were received with love and reverence, for the holy recognized the holy, and the hermits of the forest understood who it was that walked among them. Rāma and Sītā and Lakshmaṇa became, in these years, a part of the quiet world of the forest sages, sharing their simple life, their disciplines, their devotions, moving among the scattered ashrams like pilgrims who never quite settled and never quite left.

Let us try to picture that life, for it has a beauty that the crises of the story can make us forget. Imagine the rustic peace of it: the small ashrams tucked into clearings, ringed by great trees, with their sacred fires and their gardens of herbs and their tame deer wandering among the huts. Imagine the rhythm of the days, the gathering of fruit and roots, the fetching of water from clear streams, the tending of the fires, the long evenings of talk with wise old men who had spent their lives in the pursuit of truth. Imagine the seasons turning: the green flush of the rains, the cool clarity of the winter mornings, the heavy heat of the summer, the forest changing its dress through the year while the exiles moved gently through it. It was a hard life in its way, stripped of every comfort of the palace, but it was also a clean and a deep one, and there was a real happiness in it, the happiness of a life pared down to its essentials, lived among good people in the presence of one another and of the divine.

And the sages loved to have them, for more reasons than one. Rāma was a delight to them as a companion, gentle and reverent and wise beyond his years. But he was more than a companion; he was a protector. For the forest, beautiful as it was, was not safe. The sages who dwelt there lived under a constant shadow, the shadow of the rākshasas, the demons who haunted the Daṇḍaka and preyed upon the holy. The demons hated the sages and their sacrifices, hated the light and the discipline and the goodness of them, and they came in the night to defile the rites, to wreck the ashrams, and worst of all to kill and devour the hermits themselves. The sages lived in terror of them, these gentle men of prayer, unable to defend themselves, their peaceful lives shadowed always by the fear of the monstrous things that hunted them in the dark.

And so, at one of the hermitages, the sages showed Rāma a thing that fixed the purpose of his forest years, and the tellers dwell on it because it is the moment that turns the quiet exile toward its violent destiny. They led him to a place and showed him the heaped bones of ascetics, a great mound of the bones of holy men who had been killed and eaten by the rākshasas over the years, the pitiful remains of the sages’ murdered brethren, piled up as a monument to the terror under which they all lived. Look, they said in effect. Look what is done to us here. This is the fate that hangs over every one of us, every night, the fate of being torn apart and devoured by the demons who hate our prayers. We are helpless against them. We cannot fight; it is not our way; our power is in penance, not in arms. We can only pray, and die, and be added to this heap of bones. And now you have come among us, a prince, a warrior, one strong enough to stand against the darkness. Will you protect us? Will you use your strength to rid this forest of the demons that hunt us, so that the holy may live and pray in peace?

And Rāma, seeing the mound of bones, seeing the terror of the good and gentle men who had shown him such love, took a solemn vow. He vowed to protect them. He vowed to use his strength and his weapons against the demons of the forest, to stand between the sages and the darkness that hunted them, to clear the Daṇḍaka of its rākshasas so that the holy might live unafraid. It was the vow of a protector, the same principle that had governed his slaying of Tāṭakā long ago, now taken up as the great purpose of his forest years: that the strong exist to shield the weak, that the warrior’s duty is to stand between the predator and the prey, and that a prince who could protect the helpless and did not was no true prince at all.

But here the story gives us a quiet and a subtle moment, and it is Sītā who provides it, and it shows her wisdom and her love and a certain gentle prophetic unease. For Sītā, hearing Rāma take this vow, was troubled, and she spoke to him of her trouble, softly, as a wife speaks who does not wish to counsel her husband away from his duty but cannot keep silent about her fear. She reminded him of a subtle danger, a danger not of the body but of the soul. We came to the forest, she said, to live as ascetics, in peace, harming no one. And here you are vowing to take up arms, to seek out the demons and destroy them. I do not question the rightness of protecting the sages; it is a noble thing. But consider: is there not a danger in going to seek out conflict, in taking up violence even for a good cause, when we came here for peace? The very carrying of weapons, the very readiness to fight, can draw a man toward fighting, can entangle him in quarrels that need not have been his, can lead, step by step, from righteous protection into unnecessary war. I do not say do not protect the innocent. I only say: be watchful. Do not let the taking-up of arms for a good cause pull you further into conflict than the cause requires. There is a wisdom in not seeking out the fight, even when one is strong enough to win it.

It was gently said, and it was wise, and it was, the tellers note with a certain sorrow, in some sense prophetic, for the chain of events that Sītā half-feared, the entanglement in a conflict that would grow and grow, was indeed about to begin, and would lead, through one thing and another, to the very catastrophe that would engulf them all. Rāma heard her, and honoured her wisdom, and did not dismiss it, but he did not turn from his vow either, for the mound of bones was real and the sages’ terror was real and the duty of protection was, to him, not a thing that could be set aside for the sake of a quieter life. He would protect the helpless; that was settled in him; and if protecting them drew him into conflict, then he would meet the conflict when it came. And Sītā, having spoken her heart, said no more, and stood with her husband as she always stood, at the edge of the thing she had gently warned against, ready to face with him whatever her warning could not prevent.

And so the peaceful years turned, at last, toward their ending. Ten of the fourteen had passed. The exiles had lived their quiet forest life, moving among the sages, and now Rāma had bound himself to the protection of the holy against the demons, and the long peace was about to break. The story gathers itself here, at the threshold of its darkest turning, and moves the three exiles toward the place where the whole tragedy would begin, toward the beautiful banks of the Godāvarī, toward the pleasant grove of Panchavaṭī, where they would build their last forest home, and where a demoness would come out of the trees and set in motion the ruin of everything.

The Shūrpaṇakhā Episode

They came at last to Panchavaṭī, on the banks of the river Godāvarī, and it was here that they made their last and longest forest home, and it was here that the peace of the exile ended and the great tragedy began.

Panchavaṭī was beautiful, as beautiful in its way as Chitrakūṭa had been. The Godāvarī ran broad and clear nearby; the land was pleasant and fertile; there were flowering groves and singing birds and a serene loveliness over the whole place. On the advice of a sage they had met, and by Rāma’s own choosing, they settled here, and Lakshmaṇa, as at Chitrakūṭa, built them a good cottage of leaf and wood, and the three of them took up again the quiet rhythm of their forest life, in this pleasant spot by the river, with the worst of the exile, as they thought, behind them and only four more years to run. They did not know that Panchavaṭī, for all its beauty, sat near the domain of the demons, close to the outposts of a power that would soon take a terrible notice of them.

For into this peace, one day, came Shūrpaṇakhā.

She was a demoness, a rākshasī, and she was the sister of Rāvaṇa himself, the mighty lord of all the demons, the ten-headed king of Lankā, though the exiles did not yet know whose sister had wandered into their grove. She was roaming the forest, and she came upon Panchavaṭī, and she saw Rāma, and she was undone by the sight of him. For Rāma, even in his hermit’s bark and matted hair, was beautiful beyond any man she had ever seen, radiant with a beauty that was not of the ordinary world, and Shūrpaṇakhā, seeing him, was seized by a violent desire, a demon’s lust, sudden and consuming, and she resolved on the instant to have him for herself.

She was a demoness, monstrous in her true form, but she had the power to change her shape, and so she took upon herself the form of a beautiful woman, a charming and alluring maiden, and in this borrowed guise she approached Rāma and made her desire known. She proposed to him directly. She wanted him for her husband, her lover; she offered herself to him; she pressed her suit with the boldness of a creature accustomed to taking what it wanted.

And Rāma, courteous even here, even to this, put her off gently, and with a touch of humour, for he saw no need to meet her folly with cruelty. I am married, he told her, and pointed to Sītā; a married man, and devoted to my wife; I am no fit object for your desire. But my brother Lakshmaṇa there is unmarried; perhaps you should address yourself to him. He said it lightly, half in jest, wishing only to turn the demoness away without offence, not imagining that his light words would become a link in a terrible chain.

So Shūrpaṇakhā turned to Lakshmaṇa, and pressed her suit on him instead, and Lakshmaṇa, taking up his brother’s jesting tone, put her off in his turn, but with a mocking edge. Why would you want me, he said in effect, a mere servant, a slave to my brother and his wife? If you wed me you would be a servant’s wife, a poor match for one so fine as you. Better to look elsewhere than to bind yourself to a bondsman. He was mocking her, gently deflecting her as Rāma had, sending her back and forth between them, and neither brother took her seriously, and both imagined they were simply and harmlessly turning aside an absurd and unwelcome advance.

But Shūrpaṇakhā was not a woman to be mocked, and beneath the borrowed beauty she was a demoness of terrible power and terrible pride, and the sport the brothers made of her, the passing of her back and forth, the light refusals, kindled in her a rage as violent as her desire had been. She saw, or believed she saw, that she was being played with, and worse, she fixed on the cause of her rejection: Sītā. It was Sītā who stood between her and Rāma; it was that woman, that human wife, who was the obstacle to her desire. And in a flash the demoness’s lust turned to murderous fury, and her beautiful disguise fell away, and she showed her true and hideous form, and she charged at Sītā, meaning to kill her, to tear apart the rival who stood in her way, to remove by murder the obstacle to her desire.

It happened fast, as such things happen. One moment there was a charming maiden pressing an absurd suit; the next there was a monstrous demoness, revealed in all her horror, lunging at Sītā with murder in her eyes. And Lakshmaṇa, who guarded Sītā as he guarded his own life, did not hesitate. In one swift protective motion he drew his sword and struck, and he did not kill the demoness, but he mutilated her, cutting off her nose and her ears, marking her, disfiguring her, driving her back shrieking and bleeding from the grove.

Now this act, Lakshmaṇa’s swift disfigurement of Shūrpaṇakhā, is one of the pivots of the whole epic, the small violent moment from which the entire vast catastrophe unfolds, and it is worth pausing on before we let it set the avalanche in motion. Was it just? The demoness had, after all, revealed herself as a murderous monster charging at an innocent woman; to strike her down in that instant was to protect Sītā from imminent death, and that protection was Lakshmaṇa’s plain duty. And yet there is a harshness in the mutilation, a disfiguring cruelty in the cutting of nose and ears rather than a clean killing or a simple driving-off, that has troubled thoughtful readers ever since, and that the story does not entirely resolve. Perhaps it was the mockery that had preceded it, the light contempt with which the brothers had treated her, that gave the act its edge. Perhaps it was simply the swift brutal reflex of a guardian defending his charge. But whatever its justice, its consequence was enormous, for Shūrpaṇakhā was no ordinary demoness to be disfigured and forgotten; she was the sister of the lord of the demons, and she fled now, mutilated and shrieking for vengeance, straight toward the powers that would answer her injury with a war that would consume the world.

There is a lesson folded into this pivot, and it is a sobering one. The whole great tragedy that follows, the abduction, the war, the deaths of thousands, the near-destruction of everything, all of it flows from this small moment in the grove, from a demoness’s lust and two brothers’ mockery and a guardian’s swift blade. Enormous consequences can hang from tiny hinges. A light jest, an unthinking cruelty, a moment’s violence, and the avalanche begins that will not stop until a whole civilization lies in ruins. The story does not tell us that Lakshmaṇa was wrong to protect Sītā; he was not. But it shows us, with terrible clarity, how the smallest act can loose the largest catastrophe, how the mockery of a rejected creature and the disfiguring of a demoness in a quiet grove can set in motion the fall of Lankā and the deaths of numberless warriors, and it asks us to feel the weight of that, to understand that no act is small, that every stone we loose may start an avalanche we cannot call back.

Shūrpaṇakhā fled, then, mutilated and howling, out of Panchavaṭī and away toward her own people, toward her demon brothers, carrying her injury and her fury and her thirst for revenge, and behind her in the grove the three exiles stood in the sudden wreckage of their peace, not yet understanding, not yet able to understand, that the quiet years were over, that the demoness’s flight was the first stone of the avalanche, and that everything, from this moment, would move with a terrible gathering speed toward the abyss.

Kamban’s Shūrpaṇakhā

Let us pause the rushing story for the space of a single chapter, and look more closely at the demoness who has just fled the grove, for she is a more interesting figure than the swift telling has allowed, and the great poets who have sung this tale have seen her in strikingly different ways, and the difference is worth our attention.

In the telling of Vālmīki, the first and oldest singer of the Rāmāyaṇa, Shūrpaṇakhā is drawn as a creature of plain and simple monstrosity. She is hideous from the start, grotesque, her ugliness matched to her nature, a demoness whose repellent form declares her repellent soul. When she desires Rāma, it is the crude lust of a monster; when she is mocked, it is a monster’s rage; when she is disfigured, it is a monster’s shrieking. There is little in Vālmīki to complicate our judgment of her. She is an obstacle, a trigger, a grotesque, and the tale moves past her quickly to the greater matters her injury sets in motion.

But there was another great singer of this story, far to the south and many centuries later, the Tamil poet Kamban, whose Rāmāyaṇa is one of the glories of Tamil literature, and Kamban saw Shūrpaṇakhā quite differently, and drew her with a subtlety and a psychological depth that transforms the whole episode. In Kamban’s telling, Shūrpaṇakhā is not a simple grotesque. She is Kāmarūpiṇī, one who can take any form at will, and the form she takes to approach Rāma is one of ravishing, genuine, almost heartbreaking beauty. She becomes a maiden lovelier than any mortal woman, and her beauty is not a crude disguise but a true art, and her desire for Rāma is drawn not as a monster’s appetite but as something closer to a real and consuming passion, a love that overwhelms her, that makes her, for a while, almost sympathetic, almost tragic.

Consider what this does to the episode. In Kamban’s hands, the scene at Panchavaṭī becomes a subtle and dangerous drama of temptation. Here is Rāma, the perfect husband, the very ideal of fidelity, and here before him is a being who has made herself into the most beautiful woman imaginable, pressing upon him a passionate love, and the whole encounter becomes a test, a probing of Rāma’s constancy, a moment in which the temptation is real precisely because the beauty is real. The dialogue of allure, in Kamban, is a thing of genuine art, the demoness deploying every grace, every sweetness, every seduction, and Rāma turning her aside not because she is obviously monstrous, for she is not, she is exquisite, but because his fidelity is absolute, because no beauty however great can move him from Sītā. The temptation has teeth, and Rāma’s resistance means something, because he is refusing not a grotesque but a genuine and dazzling enticement.

Why does this difference matter? Why should we care that one poet drew her ugly and another drew her beautiful? Because the two portrayals ask different questions and teach different things, and both are true to something in the human situation. Vālmīki’s monstrous Shūrpaṇakhā teaches us about the ugliness of ungoverned appetite, about the way lust and rage reveal themselves in their true deformity, about evil that wears its nature on its face. Kamban’s beautiful Shūrpaṇakhā teaches us something subtler and perhaps more useful: that temptation, in this world, rarely comes to us wearing a monster’s face. It comes beautiful. It comes alluring. It comes wearing exactly the form most likely to move us, and its danger lies precisely in its beauty, in the fact that it does not look like the ruin it is. The demoness who comes as a hideous monster is easy to refuse; any fool can refuse her. The demoness who comes as the loveliest woman in the world, pressing a passionate and seemingly genuine love, is a far harder thing to turn aside, and the virtue that turns her aside is a far greater virtue. Kamban, by making her beautiful, makes Rāma’s fidelity heroic rather than merely automatic, and makes the episode a real drama of temptation and constancy rather than a simple repulsion of a grotesque.

And there is a further depth in Kamban’s portrayal, a genuine pathos, for a Shūrpaṇakhā who truly loves, who has made herself beautiful out of real longing, who is refused and then, in her exposed grief and rage, mutilated, is a more tragic figure than a mere monster. There is something almost pitiable in her, in Kamban’s telling: a being consumed by a passion she cannot help, reaching for a love that can never be hers, and destroyed for the reaching. Her transformation from the beautiful maiden of her own making back into the raging demoness of her true nature, when her love turns to fury at Sītā, is not merely the dropping of a disguise but a kind of fall, a collapse from the beauty she aspired to back into the monstrousness she came from, and there is a sorrow in it that Vālmīki’s simpler portrait does not reach.

We might set her, for a moment, beside the temptresses and the wronged women of other great epics, for this story does not exist in isolation, and the comparison lights it up. Think of the enchantresses of the Greek tales, a Circe or a Calypso, who hold heroes with their beauty and their desire; think of the women scorned whose fury drives the plots of tragedy. Shūrpaṇakhā, in Kamban’s fuller drawing, belongs in that great company: the figure of desire refused, whose refusal looses catastrophe, whose wounded passion becomes the engine of a war. For it is worth remembering, as we judge her, that the whole vast tragedy that follows flows from her, from her desire and her injury and her vengeful flight, and that she is therefore not a minor grotesque at all but one of the hinges of the entire epic, the small wounded creature whose pain sets the world aflame. The war that levels Lankā, the deaths of the great heroes on both sides, the long agony of Sītā’s captivity, all of it begins with a demoness who loved and was refused and was disfigured for it, and there is a terrible weight in that, a reminder that the great catastrophes of the world often begin not in grand villainy but in a single wounded and inflamed heart.

The tragedy of the mutilation, in Kamban’s telling, gains its full force from all of this. When Lakshmaṇa’s blade takes her nose and her ears, it is not merely the driving-off of a monster; it is the bloody disfigurement of a being who, moments before, had made herself the most beautiful thing in the forest, and the horror of it is sharpened by the beauty it destroys. The maiden who came in loveliness flees in blood and ruin, her borrowed beauty hacked away, her true monstrousness now matched by a real and hideous wound, and she carries that wound and that humiliation straight to the one being in all the world most able to avenge it: her brother, the lord of the demons.

And with that we return from our pause to the rushing current of the story, for Shūrpaṇakhā, however we choose to see her, monstrous or beautiful, villain or tragic figure, is now fleeing toward vengeance, and the small wound in the grove is about to become the wound of the world. We have lingered over her because she deserves the lingering, because the great poets thought her worth their deepest art, and because the whole of what follows hangs upon her; but the current will not wait, and it carries us now toward her brothers, and toward the first of the wars that her injury will bring.

Khara and His Army Liquidated

Shūrpaṇakhā did not flee all the way to Lankā at first. She went to nearer kin, to her brothers Khara and Dūshaṇa, demon chieftains who held the forest country of the Daṇḍaka with a great host of rākshasas at their command, ruling that wild region in their brother Rāvaṇa’s name. To them she came, bleeding and shrieking, disfigured and mad with humiliation and rage, and she flung herself before them and demanded vengeance.

She told them what had happened, but she told it as fury tells things, twisted and inflamed, to kindle their anger to match her own. She spoke of the insult, the mockery, the mutilation. She may have said little of her own lust and her own attack on Sītā that had provoked the blade; the injured seldom dwell on their own share in their injuries. She made it a matter of demon honour, of the family’s pride, of a rākshasī sister humiliated and disfigured by two human wanderers in the forest, and she demanded that her brothers avenge her, that they destroy these insolent humans and bring her the blood she thirsted for.

And Khara’s fury rose to meet hers. That his sister should be so treated, that two mere men should dare to disfigure a princess of the demon race in Khara’s own domain, was an insult he would answer in blood. He did not go himself at first; he sent a party of his warriors, fourteen of them, fierce rākshasas, to kill the humans and avenge his sister. And Rāma met them, and destroyed them, all fourteen, swiftly and utterly, so that not one returned. And Shūrpaṇakhā, seeing even these champions fall, raged the more, and taunted her brother, and demanded that he take the field himself with his whole host.

So Khara mustered his army, and it was a mighty one: fourteen thousand rākshasas, a vast host of demon warriors, the whole strength of the Daṇḍaka’s dark power, and he led them out himself, with Dūshaṇa and his other captains, to fall upon Panchavaṭī and wipe out the two brothers and take their vengeance. Fourteen thousand demons marched against one man, for it would come to that, one man against fourteen thousand, and the story means us to feel the enormity of the odds.

For Rāma, seeing the vast host approaching, did a thing that shows both his prudence and his confidence. He would not risk Sītā in a battle of such scale, and he would keep Lakshmaṇa to guard her, and he would meet the demon army himself, alone. He sent Sītā, with Lakshmaṇa to protect her, into a hidden cave, safe away from the battle, and then he took his stand alone upon the field, one man, to face the fourteen thousand.

Let us hold that image, for it is one of the great images of the epic: Rāma standing alone, bow in hand, facing an entire army of demons pouring toward him across the forest, calm, unhurried, a single figure against a host, and utterly unafraid. There is something almost beyond the human in it, and the story means there to be, for this is one of the moments when Rāma’s divinity shows through the human surface, when the man we have followed through grief and exile is revealed as something more, as a power against which even fourteen thousand demons are as nothing.

And the battle, when it came, was a thing of terrible splendour. The demon host fell upon him, and Rāma met them with his divine weapons, the astras he had received from Vishvāmitra long ago, and he loosed them into the oncoming army, and the arrows flew so fast and so many that the sky was darkened with them, and the demons fell in their hundreds and their thousands. They came at him from every side, with every weapon and every dark art, and he stood and turned them all, an unbroken storm of arrows pouring from his single bow, and wherever the arrows fell the demons died. The forest was filled with the roar of it, the war-cries and the death-screams and the crash of the great trees as they fell, and through it all the single calm figure at the centre, loosing shaft after shaft, unhurried, unwearied, unstoppable.

Khara and Dūshaṇa hurled their whole strength against him, their champions, their sorceries, their vast numbers, and it availed them nothing. One by one the demon captains fell. Dūshaṇa fell. The great host was scythed down like standing grain, fourteen thousand demons destroyed by one man in a single battle, until at last only Khara himself remained, and Khara too came against Rāma in his fury and his despair, and Khara too fell, and the whole army of the Daṇḍaka, the dark power that had terrorized the sages and heaped up their bones, lay dead upon the forest floor, destroyed utterly by the single bow of the exiled prince.

It was a staggering feat, and the story frames it as such, but we should not miss the deeper thing it accomplishes, which is not merely a display of power but the fulfillment of a vow. Remember what Rāma had sworn, at the mound of bones, to the terrified sages: that he would rid the forest of its demons, that he would protect the holy from the darkness that hunted them. Here, in the destruction of Khara’s host, that vow was made good on a massive scale. The whole demon power of the Daṇḍaka, the very force that had made the forest a place of terror for the sages, was broken in a single day, and the hermits who had lived so long in dread could breathe at last, their tormentors destroyed, their protector’s promise kept. The slaughter of the fourteen thousand was terrible, but it was the terror of a healing, the same hard arithmetic that had governed the killing of Tāṭakā long ago: that the protector must sometimes deal death on a great scale so that the innocent may live, and that the destruction of a great evil, however bloody, is finally a mercy to all it would have consumed.

And yet, and yet, we must hear beneath the triumph the note of dread that the story is sounding, for this victory, glorious as it is, is also the striking of the second stone in the avalanche. Shūrpaṇakhā’s injury was the first; the destruction of Khara’s army is the second; and each blow, struck in justice, draws the exiles deeper into the war they did not seek. For Shūrpaṇakhā, seeing even Khara and his fourteen thousand annihilated, seeing the whole nearer power of her family destroyed, did not give up her vengeance. She fled now, at last, to the farthest and greatest of her kin, across the sea to Lankā itself, to lay her injury and her fury before the one being in all the world mighty enough to answer it: her brother Rāvaṇa, the ten-headed lord of all the demons, the terror of the three worlds. And what she would say to him, and how she would turn his mind toward Sītā, would set in motion the last and greatest movement of the tragedy, the abduction that would loose the war that would end the age.

Rāma had won his battle and kept his vow and cleared the forest of its terror. But in doing so he had drawn upon himself and upon Sītā the deadly attention of a power against which even his single overwhelming bow would need the help of armies, and the wilderness peace was gone forever, and the road now ran straight toward the abyss.

The Path of Ruin

Across the southern sea stood the island kingdom of Lankā, and it was no mean or squalid place, but a city of gold, magnificent, its towers bright, its palaces heaped with the plunder of the three worlds, the seat of the mightiest power of darkness that the age had known. And in the heart of it, on a throne that the gods themselves feared to challenge, sat Rāvaṇa.

He was the lord of the rākshasas, the ten-headed king, and his power was almost beyond reckoning. Through fierce penances in his youth he had won boons that made him nearly invulnerable, secure against gods and demons and every celestial power; in his pride he had not troubled to ask protection against mere men, holding men too far beneath him to matter, and in that omission, though he did not know it, his doom was already written. He had conquered heaven and humbled its gods; he had made the powers of the cosmos tremble; he ruled his golden island in a splendour and an arrogance that no one in all the worlds had dared to challenge. And into his golden court, one day, his mutilated sister came shrieking for vengeance.

Shūrpaṇakhā flung herself before Rāvaṇa’s throne, disfigured, bleeding still, and she made her appeal, and she was cunning in the making of it, for she knew her brother, and she knew that the surest way to move him was not through pity for her wound alone but through two things nearer to his heart: his pride, and his lust.

She told him of the insult first, the disfigurement of his own sister by human hands, the affront to the honour of the demon race, the destruction of Khara and Dūshaṇa and the whole fourteen thousand by a single human archer in the Daṇḍaka. This last was calculated to alarm him, for a man who could destroy fourteen thousand rākshasas alone was a power that even Rāvaṇa could not simply ignore. But she did not dwell on the danger, for she did not wish to frighten her brother away from vengeance; she wished to inflame him toward it. And so she turned quickly to the second and sharper goad.

She told him of Sītā. And here she poured out all her art, describing the beauty of Rāma’s wife in terms designed to set Rāvaṇa’s lust ablaze. There was a woman in that forest, she told him, of a beauty beyond anything in the three worlds, beyond the loveliest of Rāvaṇa’s own queens, beyond the celestial nymphs, a woman whose beauty was such that she was a fit ornament only for the greatest of kings, wasted utterly on a mere exiled human wandering the woods. Sītā, Rāma’s wife. And she, Shūrpaṇakhā, had tried to win this jewel for her brother, and it was in that very attempt that she had been disfigured. Take her, she urged. Avenge our family’s honour and possess the most beautiful woman in the world in a single stroke. Carry off Sītā, and you strike at the human who destroyed our kin, and you gain a treasure worthy of your greatness. This is the vengeance that will satisfy both your honour and your desire.

Now there was one among Rāvaṇa’s counsellors, a demon named Akampana, or by some tellings it was Shūrpaṇakhā herself who reasoned thus, who gave Rāvaṇa a piece of strategic advice that shaped the whole course of what followed. Rāma, this counsel ran, cannot be defeated in open battle. He is too strong; he has destroyed fourteen thousand of us single-handed; to meet him in direct combat is to invite destruction. But there is another way to destroy him, a surer way. His strength is bound up with his love for Sītā; she is his heart, his weakness, the one thing whose loss would break him. Do not fight Rāma. Steal his wife. Take Sītā from him by cunning, and you will break his spirit without ever crossing his sword; you will destroy him more surely by robbing him of what he loves than any army could destroy him in battle. Aim not at his strength but at his heart.

It was shrewd and it was wicked, and it appealed to everything base in Rāvaṇa, to his lust for the woman, to his desire for vengeance, and to his cowardice, for it offered him the prize without the danger, the theft without the fight. And Rāvaṇa, in his pride and his desire, resolved upon it. He would carry off Sītā. He would take by cunning the woman his sister had described, and satisfy his lust and his vengeance together, and break the human who had dared to injure his family.

Let us look, for a moment, into the ruin that was working itself out in Rāvaṇa’s soul, for the story means us to understand him, not merely to condemn him. Rāvaṇa was not a fool, and he was not, in the ordinary sense, weak. He was mighty, learned, a great king, a devotee of Shiva, a master of the scriptures, possessed of gifts and powers that made him one of the towering figures of the age. And all of it was being poured down the drain of a single ungoverned appetite. His lust for a woman he had never seen, kindled by his sister’s description, was leading him, step by deliberate step, toward an act that would destroy him and his city and his whole race. He had every advantage, every power, every reason to leave the exiles alone and keep his golden kingdom safe. And he was throwing it all away, knowingly, for the sake of possessing a woman who was another man’s wife and who would never, could never, be his. This is the deepest lesson of Rāvaṇa, and the story returns to it again and again: that the greatest strength avails nothing against the enemy within, that a man may conquer heaven and be undone by his own desire, that the ruin of the mighty comes most often not from a stronger foe but from the ungoverned wanting in their own hearts. Rāvaṇa was setting his own foot upon the path of ruin, and he was doing it with his eyes open, choosing the theft that would doom him over the restraint that would have saved him, because his appetite was stronger than his wisdom, and that is the oldest and the deadliest of all the failures of the great.

There was a dark and plotting atmosphere in that golden court as the design took shape. Rāvaṇa’s fury and lust hardened into a plan, and the plan required an instrument, for Rāvaṇa could not simply seize Sītā by force while Rāma and Lakshmaṇa guarded her; he had seen what Rāma’s bow could do. He needed cunning; he needed a trick to draw the brothers away from her, to leave her for a moment unguarded, so that he could snatch her and be gone before her protectors could prevent it. And for such a trick he needed a particular kind of servant, a demon skilled in sorcery and illusion, one who could take a false shape and play a false part.

And Rāvaṇa knew exactly whom he would compel to the task, though the demon in question would beg and warn and try with all his terrified soul to turn his master from the path. He would summon Mārīcha, the sorcerer, the shape-changer, the one demon in all Lankā who had felt the power of Rāma’s arrows before and lived, and who knew, as Rāvaṇa in his blind pride did not, exactly what doom the lord of the demons was preparing to bring down upon them all.

The Golden Stag

Rāvaṇa flew to the dwelling of Mārīcha, the demon sorcerer, and laid his design before him, and commanded his help. And Mārīcha, hearing what was asked of him, was seized with a terror that the whole rest of the chapter turns upon, for Mārīcha, alone among Rāvaṇa’s servants, knew Rāma from bitter experience, and knew that the path his master proposed led straight to destruction.

For Mārīcha had felt Rāma’s power before, long ago. He it was, the reader may remember, whom the young Rāma had struck at the sacrifice of Vishvāmitra, when Rāma, sparing his life, had loosed a weapon that hurled him bodily across the miles and flung him into the distant sea. Mārīcha had never forgotten it. The memory of that blow, of the effortless overwhelming power of the boy who had tossed him across the world like a pebble, had branded itself into his soul, and had turned him, in the years since, from a marauding demon into something almost like a hermit, a demon who had withdrawn from his old violence and lived quietly in the forest, precisely because he had learned what Rāma was and wanted never again to come within reach of that terrible bow.

And now his master was commanding him to go and provoke that very power, to place himself once more in Rāma’s path, and Mārīcha was filled with a dread that made him bold, bold enough to argue with the lord of the demons, to warn him, to plead with him, at the risk of his own life, to turn from the path of ruin.

He warned Rāvaṇa with all the desperate eloquence of terror. Do not do this, he begged. You do not know what Rāma is. I know. I have felt his power. He is no ordinary man; he is death itself in human form; to cross him is to embrace destruction. I tell you, I who have been thrown across the world by his arrow and have lived every day since in the shadow of that memory: leave him alone. Leave his wife alone. Take your golden kingdom and your great power and your queens and be content, and do not, for the sake of a single woman, bring down upon yourself and all of Lankā the doom that this Rāma will surely deal you. You imagine you are planning a clever theft. You are planning the destruction of your race. I have seen his strength; you have not; believe me, and turn back, before you loose upon us all a ruin that nothing will be able to stop.

He spoke, the tellers say, as one who saw the future clearly, and in a sense he did, for every word of his warning would come true. But Rāvaṇa would not hear it. His pride could not brook being counselled by a servant, and his lust and his fury were beyond the reach of reason, and Mārīcha’s very terror only angered him, for it implied that there was a power in the world greater than Rāvaṇa’s own, and that his proud soul could not accept.

And so Rāvaṇa gave Mārīcha a choice, and it was the choice of a tyrant, no choice at all. Serve me in this, he said, or die by my hand, here, now, for your refusal. If you will not go and play your part in my design, I will kill you myself, this instant, for your cowardice and your insolence. Choose: obey me, or die.

Here is the cruel hinge of Mārīcha’s fate, and the story dwells on it because it is a genuine moral situation, terrible and clarifying. Mārīcha was offered death either way. If he refused Rāvaṇa, he would die at once, murdered by his own master for his disobedience, an ignoble death, a coward’s execution. If he obeyed Rāvaṇa, he would go and provoke Rāma, and he was certain, being wiser than his master, that this too would mean his death, for Rāma would surely kill him. Death behind him, death before him; the only question was which death to choose.

And Mārīcha, facing it, chose with a strange and bitter dignity. If I must die, he reasoned, let me die at the hands of Rāma rather than at the hands of this tyrant. Death from that divine bow is a nobler end than death from a demon’s spite; to be slain by Rāma is almost a liberation, a release from this wretched existence at the hands of the very power I have feared and, in fearing, half- worshipped, all these years. Better to die by the arrow of the divine than by the blow of the wicked. If I must perish, let it be Rāma who kills me, and let my death at least be at worthy hands.

There is a real pathos in this, and the story feels it. Mārīcha is not a good being; he is a demon, a servant of evil, a creature who has done wickedness in his time. And yet in this moment he is granted a kind of grim nobility, for he sees the truth that his master is blind to, he speaks it at the risk of his life, and when he is overborne he chooses the nobler of two deaths with a clear and bitter courage. He goes to his doom knowingly, understanding exactly what he does, choosing to be the instrument of a design he knows is ruinous only because the alternative is a meaner death, and finding, in the certainty of dying by Rāma’s hand, something almost like grace. He is a damned creature who sees his damnation clearly, and there is a tragic dignity in the clear- sightedness, a dignity denied to his master, who rushes toward the same doom blind and proud.

So Mārīcha yielded. Compelled by the certainty of death either way, and choosing the death that came from the divine over the death that came from the tyrant, he agreed to play his part in Rāvaṇa’s design. And the part was this: he would use his sorcery to take the form of a deer, but no ordinary deer, a deer of impossible, dazzling, unnatural beauty, a golden stag with a hide that shone like gold and silver, spotted with jewels, its eyes like gems, a creature so lovely and so strange that no one who saw it could fail to desire it. He would appear at Panchavaṭī in this enchanting shape, and dance and graze near the cottage, and by his unnatural beauty he would draw Sītā’s longing, and through Sītā’s longing he would draw Rāma away in pursuit, and so the guard on Sītā would be broken, and Rāvaṇa’s moment would come.

It was a cunning and a wicked plan, and it turned upon the one weakness that even the wise and the good can share: the pull of beauty, the longing for the lovely thing glimpsed and desired. And Mārīcha, going to his death with open eyes, took upon himself the golden shape, and turned his steps toward Panchavaṭī, toward the cottage by the Godāvarī where Sītā sat unknowing, to lure her, and her husband, and the whole world, toward the abyss.

The Good Bird Jaṭāyu

The golden stag came to Panchavaṭī in the bright of day, and it was as lovely as Mārīcha’s sorcery could make it, and Sītā saw it, and was enchanted.

It moved at the edge of the grove, grazing, its golden hide catching the sunlight and throwing it back in a shimmer, its jewelled spots gleaming, its whole form so impossibly beautiful that it seemed less an animal than a wonder out of a dream. Sītā, gathering flowers near the cottage, looked up and saw it and was caught, as anyone might be caught, by the sheer dazzling loveliness of the thing. She had never seen its like; no one had; and a longing rose in her to have it, to keep it, to possess so beautiful a creature. She called to Rāma and Lakshmaṇa to come and see, and she begged Rāma to catch it for her, to take it alive if he could so that she might keep it, or if not, at least to bring her its marvellous golden hide.

Now Lakshmaṇa, ever watchful, ever suspicious, distrusted the creature at once. This is no natural animal, he warned. A golden deer, jewelled, shining? There is no such beast in all the world. It is some trick, some illusion, some demon’s snare; I have never liked the sorceries of this forest, and this reeks of them. Do not chase it, brother. It is a trap. And Rāma himself felt the same unease, and said as much; he too sensed something unnatural in the creature, something that did not belong to the ordinary order of the world.

But Sītā’s longing was strong, and here the story places its finger, gently and without harshness, on the small human weakness that opens the door to catastrophe. Sītā was not foolish, and she was not weak; she was the wisest and strongest of women, as the whole story has shown. But she wanted the beautiful thing, wanted it with the simple immediate longing that beauty kindles in us, and her wanting overrode the caution that both her husband and her brother-in-law urged upon her. She pressed Rāma. She would not be dissuaded. And Rāma, who loved her, and who could refuse her little, and who reasoned that even if the creature were a demon he was more than able to deal with it, at last gave way to her wish. He would go and catch or kill the golden stag. But he was uneasy still, and he gave Lakshmaṇa a strict charge before he went: stay here, he said, guard Sītā, do not leave her side for any reason, whatever happens. And with that he took up his bow and went after the deer.

The stag led him a long chase. That was Mārīcha’s art; the creature did not simply flee but lured, staying always just ahead, drawing Rāma deeper and deeper into the forest, farther and farther from the cottage, until the pursuit had carried him a great distance from Panchavaṭī and from Sītā. And when at last Rāma, wearying of the chase and certain now that the thing was no true animal, drew his bow and loosed a shaft that struck the golden stag down, the demon’s final and most treacherous stroke was played.

For Mārīcha, dying, reverting in his death-throes to his true demon form, used the last of his sorcery to work the ruin he had been sent to work. He cried out, and he cried out in Rāma’s own voice, perfectly mimicked, a cry of anguish and distress: Ah, Sītā! Ah, Lakshmaṇa! as though Rāma himself were stricken, wounded, calling desperately for help. The false cry rang through the forest in Rāma’s very tones, and then Mārīcha died, his part played, his death exactly the death he had foreseen and chosen, at the hands of Rāma, and the trap was sprung.

The cry reached the cottage, and it reached Sītā, and it undid her. For it was Rāma’s voice, or seemed to be, crying out in mortal distress, and Sītā’s heart turned over with terror for her husband. She turned to Lakshmaṇa and begged him, commanded him, to go at once to Rāma’s aid, for surely Rāma was in danger, surely that was his cry of pain, surely he needed help or he would not have called.

And Lakshmaṇa, torn now between two duties, hesitated, and his hesitation was wisdom, and it was overborne. He knew Rāma. He knew that no danger in that forest could wring such a cry from his brother, that Rāma was beyond the power of any demon to reduce to such a helpless scream, that the cry must therefore be a trick, an illusion, a snare exactly like the golden stag itself. And he knew, too, his charge: to guard Sītā and not to leave her. He tried to reason with her, to calm her, to tell her that the cry was surely false, that Rāma was in no danger, that it was a demon’s trick to draw them out, that he must not leave her side.

But Sītā, in her terror for Rāma, would not be calmed, and here she spoke words that she would regret to the end of her days, words that were unjust and cruel, wrung from her by fear. She turned on Lakshmaṇa in her panic and accused him. Why do you delay, she cried, why do you refuse to help your brother? Do you wish him dead? Is that it? Do you covet me, that you would let Rāma die so that you might have me for yourself? Is that why you cling to my side and will not go to him? She flung these terrible accusations at the most loyal of men, the brother who had given up everything to serve Rāma, who guarded her honour as his own, and the injustice of them was staggering, and they came from a place of pure unreasoning terror, and they wounded Lakshmaṇa to the soul. We should feel the pity of this, for no one here is truly at fault, and that is the deepest sorrow of it. Sītā’s cruel words came not from any wickedness but from a wife’s blind terror for her husband; she was not herself; fear had unmade her judgment. And Lakshmaṇa’s yielding came not from any weakness but from the impossible position she had put him in, for how could he stay at the side of a woman who was accusing him of the vilest motives, who was commanding him in the name of his brother’s life to go? The accusation made his staying unbearable and his going a kind of forced obedience. He was trapped between his charge to guard her and the intolerable thing she had made of his guarding.

At last, stung beyond bearing and unable to remain, Lakshmaṇa yielded. But before he went, he did what he could to protect her. He drew, the tellers say, a line upon the ground around the cottage, a boundary, the Lakshmaṇa Rekhā, and he charged Sītā with all his earnestness never to cross it, never to step beyond that protective line, for within it she would be safe, and beyond it lay danger. And having drawn the line and made her promise, and having reproached her gently for her cruel words, and having called on the powers of the forest to guard her, Lakshmaṇa went, against his own judgment, against his charge, driven out by Sītā’s terror and her unjust accusation, to seek his brother.

And the cottage was left unguarded, which was the whole aim of the trick, and no sooner was Lakshmaṇa gone than the last player in the design appeared. Rāvaṇa came. He had watched and waited, and now, with Rāma lured away and Lakshmaṇa driven off, he came to the cottage, but not in his own terrible form; he came disguised as a wandering ascetic, a holy man, a harmless mendicant begging alms, in saffron robes, with a staff and a begging bowl, the very image of sanctity.

And Sītā, alone, seeing what appeared to be a holy man at the edge of the grove asking for alms, was caught by the oldest and gentlest of obligations, the duty of hospitality, the sacred rule that a guest, above all a holy guest, must be received and fed and never turned away. It would have been a sin, by everything she had been taught, to refuse a holy mendicant. And so, to offer him food, trusting his holy appearance, bound by the law of hospitality, she stepped across the line that Lakshmaṇa had drawn.

And the instant she crossed it, the disguise fell away. The ascetic became the demon, the ten-headed lord of Lankā in his full and terrible power, and before Sītā could flee or cry out he seized her, and lifted her, and rose into the air in his aerial chariot, bearing her away, up and away over the forest, southward, toward the sea and Lankā, while she screamed and struggled helplessly in his grasp and the empty forest echoed with her cries.

The trap had closed. The golden stag, the false cry, the driven-off guardian, the holy disguise, the crossed line, every piece of the cunning wicked design had done its work, and Sītā was taken, borne away through the sky by the lord of the demons, and the whole vast tragedy that Mārīcha had foreseen and Rāvaṇa had refused to fear was now, irrevocably, set loose upon the world.

Closely Guarded

Sītā did not go silently into the sky, and her cries were heard, and one who heard them answered, and the answer is one of the noblest and most moving episodes in the whole epic.

For as Rāvaṇa flew southward with his struggling captive, his path carried him over the domain of an old and mighty bird, Jaṭāyu, the great vulture, a creature of enormous age and enormous nobility, who had been in his youth a friend of King Dasharatha himself, and who therefore held Rāma and all his house in love and loyalty. Jaṭāyu heard the cries. He saw the ten-headed demon flying through the sky bearing away a weeping woman, and he saw that the woman was Sītā, the wife of Rāma, the daughter-in-law, as it were, of his own old friend the dead king, and though he was aged, though his strength was long past its prime, though he must have known that he was no match for the lord of all the demons, Jaṭāyu did not hesitate for an instant. He rose into the air to bar Rāvaṇa’s path, and he challenged him, and he gave battle.

Let us honour what the old bird did, for it is pure heroism, the heroism of the hopeless stand, the courage that fights not because it can win but because it must not stand aside. Jaṭāyu was old. Rāvaṇa was the mightiest being of the age, the conqueror of heaven, nearly invulnerable, in the full flush of his power. There was no chance, none, that the aged vulture could defeat him. Jaṭāyu knew it. And he attacked anyway, because before him a helpless woman was being carried off to a terrible fate, because she was the wife of one he loved, because to see such a wrong and do nothing would have been a betrayal of everything he was, and because some wrongs must be resisted even when the resistance is certain to fail. That is the essence of his heroism: not the hope of victory, but the refusal, whatever the cost, to let the evil pass unopposed.

And he fought magnificently. Old as he was, he flung himself upon Rāvaṇa with a fury that for a while actually checked the demon, tearing at him with beak and talon, ripping at his flesh, savaging his chariot, breaking his bow, killing the demon steeds that drew the aerial car, casting Rāvaṇa down to the earth and forcing him to fight for his life. For a time the aged vulture, fighting for the honour of his dead friend’s house, actually had the better of the lord of the demons, and it seemed almost that heroism and right might triumph against all odds.

But they did not, for Rāvaṇa’s power was too great, and the odds were, in the end, exactly as hopeless as they had appeared. Rāvaṇa recovered himself, and drew his sword, and in the fury of the battle he struck at the old bird and cut off his wings, and Jaṭāyu, maimed, his great pinions severed, fell at last out of the sky and crashed to the earth, mortally wounded, his heroic stand ended, his strength poured out, dying. And Rāvaṇa, freed of his one opponent, gathered up the terrified Sītā again and flew on toward Lankā, leaving the old bird broken and bleeding on the forest floor.

But Jaṭāyu did not die at once. He clung to life, there on the ground where he had fallen, holding on by sheer will, because he had one thing left to do, one last service to render, and he would not let go of life until he had done it: he would live long enough to tell Rāma what had happened, to name the demon, to point the way, so that his death should not be in vain. And so he lay there, dying by inches, waiting, holding the knowledge that Rāma would need.

And Sītā, borne away helpless through the sky, did what little was in her power to do, and it was a small thing and a wise one, and it would matter greatly in time. As Rāvaṇa carried her over the forests and toward the sea, she saw below her, on the summit of a mountain, a group of monkeys, vānaras, watching, and in that instant she thought quickly. She gathered together some of her ornaments, her jewels, and bundled them in a piece of her garment, in her silken upper cloth, and she let the bundle drop, casting it down toward the watching monkeys, so that it fell among them on the mountaintop. It was a message, a clue, a trail; she could not free herself, she could not send word, but she could leave a sign, a token that might one day tell searchers which way she had been taken. It was the act of a clear mind even in the extremity of terror, and it was exactly the kind of quiet resourcefulness that Sītā had shown all along, and those dropped jewels would indeed, in time, become a thread that helped lead her rescuers to her.

So Rāvaṇa bore her at last across the sea to Lankā, to his golden city, and there he set her down, and there her long captivity began. But he could not make her his, and this is the thing to understand about that captivity: that even in his power, even carried off to his island fortress, even wholly in his physical grip, Sītā was not conquered, and Rāvaṇa could not touch her. For Rāvaṇa, mighty as he was, was bound by an old curse that prevented him from forcing any woman against her will, and so he could not simply take Sītā; he could only try to win her consent, to persuade her, to break her spirit until she yielded of her own accord. And that consent he would never, never get.

He did not imprison her in a dungeon, but in a grove, the Ashokavana, a garden of ashoka trees within his palace grounds, a place of some beauty, and there he set her, surrounded and guarded, but guarded by a horror: a company of fierce and hideous rākshasīs, demon-women, ogresses, set to watch over her day and night, to threaten her, to torment her, to wear down her resistance with their menaces and their cruelty, to guard her closely so that she could not escape and could not be rescued, and to labour without cease at the breaking of her will. Closely guarded she was, ringed by monstrous keepers, cut off from all the world, a prisoner in a garden, in the heart of the enemy’s golden city, across a sea from any hope of help.

And there we must leave her for now, in the Ashokavana, ringed by her monstrous guards, grieving for Rāma, holding fast to her love and her honour against all the menace of her captors, unshakable in the midst of her helplessness, the most closely guarded captive in all the three worlds. She did not yet know whether Rāma even lived, or whether he knew where she was, or whether any rescue could ever reach her across that terrible sea. She knew only that she would not yield, that she would die before she would consent to Rāvaṇa, that her heart was Rāma’s and would remain his though the whole power of Lankā were arrayed to break her. And in that unbreakable fidelity, held fast in the very citadel of the enemy, lay the seed of Rāvaṇa’s doom, though the demon king, in his pride and his lust, could not yet see it.

Far to the north, in the forest, Rāma was even now returning to the empty cottage, all unknowing, to find his wife gone, and to begin the long descent into a grief that would nearly destroy him, before it forged him into the instrument of Lankā’s ruin.

Rāma Disconsolate

Rāma came back through the forest with a growing dread in his heart. The golden stag had been a demon, as he had feared; the false cry in his own voice had told him that some trick was afoot; and as he hurried back toward the cottage he met Lakshmaṇa coming to find him, and the sight of his brother, who should have been guarding Sītā, filled him with a terror he could not yet name. Why have you left her, he demanded. Why are you here, when I charged you never to leave her side? And Lakshmaṇa, wretched, told him: of the cry in Rāma’s voice, of Sītā’s terror, of her cruel accusation, of how she had driven him out against his own judgment and his own charge. And the two of them, cold with fear now, ran together toward the cottage.

They found it empty.

Sītā was gone. The cottage stood open and silent, and there was no sign of her but the signs of violence and disorder, and Rāma, standing in the empty doorway of the home where he had left his wife, understood that the worst had happened, that she had been taken, that the whole cunning design of stag and cry and crossed line had been aimed at exactly this, and that he had walked straight into it, and that Sītā was gone.

And here the story shows us something it has not shown us before, for through everything that had come, the loss of the crown, the exile, the death of his father, Rāma had held to his great calm, had borne every blow with a serenity that seemed almost beyond the human. But this blow broke through. This he could not bear with composure. For this was Sītā, his wife, his other self, the companion who had refused to be left behind, who had followed him into the wilderness for love, and she was gone, taken, carried off to some unknown fate, and the calm that had carried Rāma through every other sorrow shattered against the enormity of this one, and Rāma grieved as men grieve, wildly, helplessly, almost to the edge of madness.

He searched. He ran through the forest calling her name. He looked in every direction, in the cottage, in the grove, along the river, everywhere, as though she might yet be found, as though the horror might yet be undone if only he searched hard enough. And when the searching found nothing, he began to speak to the forest itself, in his anguish, in the derangement of his grief. He asked the trees if they had seen her. He begged the deer to tell him which way she had gone. He questioned the river, the flowers, the birds, the very rocks, crying out to the unanswering wilderness for word of his lost wife, half out of his mind with sorrow, a great and dignified man reduced by grief to pleading with the insensible world.

Let us not look away from this, for the story does not, and there is something important in its refusal to spare Rāma this collapse. We have followed a Rāma who seemed almost too perfect, too calm, too unshakable, a man who could lose a kingdom without a tremor. And now we see him broken, wild with grief, talking to the trees, and the sight makes him human to us in a way that all his serene virtue never quite did. For this is the meaning of the incarnation, the thing the story insisted upon at the very beginning: that the divine, in taking human form, took on human grief truly, not as a performance, not as a god pretending to suffer, but really, to the bottom, so that there is no sorrow of ours that he has not felt. Rāma’s madness of grief in the empty forest is the proof of it. He loved as we love, and he lost as we lose, and he grieved as we grieve, past all his philosophy, past all his composure, with the raw helpless anguish of any husband whose wife has been torn from him. The perfect calm was real, but so is this; and the two together are the whole truth of him, the man who could bear anything for duty and yet could be broken by love, exactly as we are broken.

And it fell to Lakshmaṇa now to be the strong one, and this too is worth marking, for it reverses the order we have seen all along. Through the whole story it has been Rāma who was calm and Lakshmaṇa who was passionate, Rāma who steadied and Lakshmaṇa who raged. But now, in the depth of Rāma’s grief, Lakshmaṇa became the steady one, the anchor, the voice of reason and resolve. He grieved too, and he carried besides the terrible weight of his own guilt, for it was his leaving that had opened the door to the abduction, though the fault was not truly his. But he set his own grief and guilt aside to hold his brother up. Do not despair, brother, he urged. Grief will not bring her back; grief will only unman you when you most need your strength. She has been taken, yes, but taken is not lost; she may yet be found; she may yet be rescued. Master your sorrow. Turn it into resolve. We will search, we will find who has done this, we will follow, and we will get her back. But you must be Rāma again; you must not drown in this; for her sake, if she is to be saved, you must be strong. And by such words Lakshmaṇa slowly drew his brother back from the edge of the abyss of grief, back toward purpose, back toward the resolve that alone could save Sītā if she could be saved at all.

There is a deep human truth in this reversal, and it is one worth carrying away. Even the strongest among us have their breaking point, the one loss that overwhelms even the greatest composure; and in that moment, the strength we need may have to come from another, from one who is ordinarily the weaker, who finds in our extremity the strength to be, for once, the steady one. Rāma had steadied Lakshmaṇa a hundred times; now Lakshmaṇa steadied Rāma; and this is how it is meant to be among those who love one another, that the strength passes back and forth as it is needed, that no one has to be strong alone all the time, that in our worst hour someone who loves us can carry us until we can carry ourselves again. Lakshmaṇa carried Rāma through the worst of that grief, and slowly Rāma came back to himself, the wild sorrow hardening into a cold and steady resolve, the resolve that would carry him across a subcontinent and over a sea and through a war to recover what had been taken from him.

So Rāma mastered his grief, or bent it to his purpose, and the two brothers set out to search in earnest, to find some trace of Sītā, some sign of which way she had been carried, some clue to the identity of the demon who had taken her. And almost at once, as they searched southward, the direction Rāvaṇa had flown, they came upon a terrible sight: signs of a great struggle in the sky and on the earth, scattered feathers, broken weapons, and there, among the wreckage, an enormous bird, mortally wounded, his wings severed, lying in his own blood at the point of death, but living still, clinging to life by will alone, waiting, it seemed, for them to come. It was Jaṭāyu, and he had held to life through his agony for exactly this, to give Rāma the word that would send him after Sītā.

A Second Father Dies

Rāma came to the dying bird, and at first, in his grief and his wariness, he did not know him, and seeing an enormous bloodied creature amid the signs of struggle, he half-took it for the demon that had done the deed. But Jaṭāyu spoke, and with his failing breath he told them who he was, and what had happened, and the truth turned Rāma’s wariness to grief and gratitude at once.

I am Jaṭāyu, the old bird said, or such were the words his ebbing strength could shape. I was the friend of your father Dasharatha; I knew him long ago; I loved your house. And I saw the demon carry off your Sītā through the sky, and I fought him, old as I am, to save her. I fought him and I could not prevail, for he was too mighty, and he cut off my wings and cast me down, and I am dying. But I lived long enough to tell you this: it was Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākshasas, the king of Lankā, who took her; and he carried her southward, toward his island kingdom across the sea. Go south, Rāma. Seek her in Lankā. That is where she is, and that is who has her, and now that I have told you, my work is done, and I can die.

And Rāma, hearing this, understanding that this broken and dying creature had given its life in the attempt to save his wife, that this old bird had thrown itself against the lord of all the demons for love of Rāma’s house and for the honour of a helpless woman, was overcome. The bird that lay dying before him had done what Rāma himself had not been there to do; had fought for Sītā when Rāma was away; had spent its last strength and its very life in her defence. And Rāma knelt down beside the dying Jaṭāyu and gathered the great broken bird into his arms, and tended him, and wept over him, and honoured him with a tenderness that is among the most moving things in the whole epic.

For consider what Jaṭāyu was to Rāma in that moment. He was his father’s friend, a link to the dead Dasharatha, almost a father himself in his age and his love. And he was dying, as Dasharatha had died, in a kind of service to Rāma, giving his life in Rāma’s cause. And so Rāma, cradling the old bird, treated him not as a beast, not even merely as a helper, but as a second father, as one worthy of a son’s deepest love and a son’s last offices. He held him as he might have held Dasharatha, had he been there to hold his father in his dying; he gave to Jaṭāyu the grief and the reverence he had not been able to give to his own father, whose death had come while Rāma was far away in the forest. In tending the dying bird, Rāma was, in a way, tending the father he had lost, performing at last the last loving service he had been robbed of the chance to perform.

And when Jaṭāyu died, his message delivered, his duty done, released at last from the agony he had held onto life through, Rāma performed for him the full funeral rites, the rites due to a father, the rites of the highest honour. He built the pyre with his own hands. He spoke the sacred words. He gave the noble bird the cremation of a king, of a kinsman, of a beloved father, and he grieved for him as a son grieves. This was no small thing, and the story means us to feel its greatness: that Rāma, a prince of the highest line, gave the full and loving funeral honours of a father to a bird, to a creature that the proud of the world would have thought beneath their notice, because that bird had shown a love and a courage and a sacrifice that made it worthy of every honour a son could give.

Here again we see the thing that runs all through Rāma’s story, the thing that made the common people love him and the forest hunters love him and the sages love him: that Rāma saw the soul and not the station, that greatness of heart was to him the only greatness that counted, and that he gave his deepest reverence not according to birth or rank or form but according to love and virtue and sacrifice. A hunter-chief, a fallen demon freed from a curse, an old vulture dying for a stranger’s wife, these were to Rāma more truly noble than many a proud king, and he honoured them accordingly, without a trace of the condescension that lesser great men show to those beneath them. Jaṭāyu was a bird, and Rāma gave him a father’s funeral, and in doing so Rāma showed once more the boundless and level compassion that was the deepest mark of his divinity, the love that knew nothing of the barriers of form and rank that divide the world.

And the death of Jaṭāyu marks something in the shape of the story, a turning, a threshold. For with the old bird’s dying words, Rāma now knew the truth: he knew who had taken Sītā, and he knew where she had been carried. The blind grief of the empty cottage, the helpless not-knowing, was over; now there was a name, Rāvaṇa, and a direction, south, and a purpose that could be pursued. The abduction had plunged Rāma into a darkness of not-knowing; Jaṭāyu’s sacrifice lifted that darkness, gave the grief an object and the search a direction, and turned Rāma from a man wandering distraught in an empty forest into a man with an enemy to find and a captive to rescue and a road, however long and terrible, to walk. The old bird’s last gift was not only the naming of the enemy but the giving of a purpose, and it was purpose, more than anything, that Rāma needed to climb up out of his grief.

There is a further grief folded into this chapter, quiet beneath the loud one, and it is worth naming. In losing his father and now, in a sense, this second father, Rāma was being stripped, one by one, of the older generation, of the fathers and protectors who had stood between him and the full weight of the world. Dasharatha was gone. Now Jaṭāyu, his father’s friend, was gone. The elders who had loved and guarded him were falling away, and Rāma was being left more and more alone to bear his burdens, to be himself the protector rather than the protected, the one who must act rather than the one who is shielded. It is a passage every life comes to, this falling-away of the older generation, this finding of oneself suddenly in the front rank with no one ahead, and Rāma came to it here, in the forest, beside the pyre of an old bird who had loved his father, and he took up, with the death of this second father, the full and lonely weight of the task that now lay before him.

Then, the rites completed, the old bird honoured and burned and mourned, Rāma and Lakshmaṇa turned their faces south, in the direction Jaṭāyu had named, toward Lankā, toward Rāvaṇa, toward the recovery of Sītā, and they went on into the deeper forest, seeking the road and the allies that would carry them toward the war that now, at last, had a direction and a name.

Left Eyelids Throb

As the brothers pressed southward through the wild, they met another of the forest’s monsters, and as with Virādha, the monster proved to be a cursed soul in disguise, and its slaying proved to be a liberation, and its dying proved to be a signpost pointing the way onward.

His name was Kabandha, and he was a horror to look upon: a huge, headless thing, a monstrous trunk with a great mouth set in its belly and a single eye, and immensely long arms with which it seized whatever came within reach and drew it to that devouring mouth. It caught Rāma and Lakshmaṇa in its terrible arms, one in each, and drew them toward its maw, and for a moment the two brothers, who had faced armies, were in real peril from this grotesque and mindless-seeming thing. But they kept their heads, and each of them, with his sword, cut off one of the monster’s great arms, freeing themselves, and so overcame it.

And as Kabandha lay dying, the same wonder happened that had happened with Virādha: the monstrous shape fell away, and a being of light rose out of it, freed from a curse.
